content.text: Angular never watches your fields. It updates the screen in passes: something notifies it that state may have changed, it walks the component tree, re-evaluates the templates that need checking, and touches only the DOM whose values differ from the last render. In Angular 22, which is zoneless and OnPush by default, a plain field assigned in a promise callback notifies nothing, so state that changes after async work belongs in a signal.

The belief: Angular watches your component's fields, so
is all it takes, and the DOM updates the moment the value changes.
For years, that's exactly what it looked like. With zone.js, which captures async operations like

, network requests and event listeners, Angular ran change detection after each of them, so an assignment in a callback reached the screen almost instantly. Some other frameworks really do track property writes, through proxies or compiled setters, which makes the model feel universal. The half-truth is that the screen did update after async work. A watcher was never the reason, though; zone.js was, and Angular 22 apps don't load it by default.
Change detection is a pass, not a watcher
Angular remembers the last value each template binding rendered. A

pass walks the component tree from the top. For each component it checks, it re-evaluates the template's expressions, compares each result with the remembered value, and updates only the DOM nodes whose value changed. Between passes, Angular doesn't look at your fields at all.
is a plain JavaScript property write: no proxy, no setter, nothing that tells Angular it happened.
Something has to schedule the pass
So the question is never "did the value change?" but "did anything tell Angular to check?" With zone.js, the answer was yes after almost every async task. Since Angular 21, new apps are

OnPush decides which components get checked

A scheduled pass doesn't check everything either. Since Angular 22, components default to OnPush, and a pass checks an OnPush component only when it was marked: a signal its template reads changed, it received a new input value, or an event fired in it or one of its children. Unmarked components are skipped. The old check-on-every-pass behavior still exists as

Dev mode checks your templates twice
In development, Angular runs an extra verification pass after each change detection pass and throws NG0100 (

) if a binding's value changed in between. It's the other side of the same model: Angular renders whatever your templates return during a pass, and it expects reading them not to change anything. A getter that returns
, or a child that updates its parent's state while it's being checked, trips it. Production builds skip this check.
